candidates.attacker_control: Any authenticated API user controls the `currentDir`, `name`/`fileName`, `suffix`, `content` and file-upload fields of POST /dolphinscheduler/resources/directory, POST /dolphinscheduler/resources, POST /dolphinscheduler/resources/online-create and PUT /dolphinscheduler/resources/{id} (ResourcesController lines 119-156, 389-405), plus GET /dolphinscheduler/resources/{id}/download (line 446). No project/admin permission is required to create a resource: verifyPid only checks parent ownership when pid != -1, and pid=-1 (root) is accepted (ResourcesServiceImpl lines 944-958). The attacker also controls the uploaded file name, so the extension-consistency check is trivially satisfied (e.g. alias `../../../../opt/dolphinscheduler/conf/dolphinscheduler_env.sh` with an uploaded `x.sh`).
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked for -- but did not find -- any name/path validation: verifyResourceName (725-755) only queries DB/storage existence; verifyFile/upload (444-480, 556-564) only compare file extensions; RegexUtils (api/utils/RegexUtils.java) contains no resource-name validator (only isValidLinuxUserName and escapeNRT log escaping). HadoopUtils.getHdfsFileName strips only one leading '/' and concatenates. Hadoop Path normalization resolves `..` rather than rejecting it, so normalization enables rather than blocks the traversal. Resource creation is not admin-gated (verifyPid skips the parent check for pid=-1). Note the existence check can block pointing a new record at an already-existing storage path, and the feature is disabled by default via `resource.storage.type=NONE`; overwrite of existing local files is still possible where the storage FS differs from the local FS, and creation of new files is always possible where the process has write permission.
candidates.impact: Escalation from ordinary API user to file-system/storage control: (a) arbitrary file creation/overwrite and recursive deletion outside the user's tenant directory in the configured resource storage (HDFS/S3/local `file:///`), crossing tenant boundaries and tampering with other users' resources; (b) arbitrary local file write with attacker-chosen content and extension on the API host via the download flow, and on worker hosts via the resource-download flow, allowing overwrite of DolphinScheduler scripts/environment files (e.g. conf/dolphinscheduler_env.sh, bin/*.sh) or user shell files, which can result in code execution as the API/worker process user and compromise of data accessible to it; (c) aggravation: the download endpoint has no ownership/project check, so any authenticated user can trigger the copy for any resource id.
candidates.prerequisites: (1) Authenticated account (any role) with API access. (2) Resource upload enabled: `resource.storage.type` must be HDFS or S3 (`PropertyUtils.getResUploadStartupState()`; note the shipped default in dolphinscheduler-common/src/main/resources/common.properties is NONE, so this feature must be configured, which is the normal production setup). (3) Target path must be writable by the API/worker process user or by the configured HDFS user; the storage path must not already exist for resource creation (existence check in verifyResourceName), while the local download target may be overwritten because copyHdfsToLocal uses overwrite=true. (4) For the worker write, a task definition must reference the traversing resource (attacker's own task is sufficient).
candidates.root_cause: Resource names and directories are used to build filesystem/storage paths with no validation or normalization. ResourcesController passes raw request parameters (currentDir, name/fileName, suffix) to ResourcesServiceImpl, which concatenates them into `fullName` (lines 112, 189, 892-893) and stores the same user-chosen string as the resource alias. These strings are then concatenated into storage paths by HadoopUtils.getHdfsFileName (dolphinscheduler-common .../HadoopUtils.java lines 542-546, only strips one leading '/') and into local paths by FileUtils.getDownloadFilename (dolphinscheduler-common .../FileUtils.java lines 48-57, uses the alias verbatim) without a `..`/separator check anywhere. verifyFile/upload only enforce that the uploaded file's extension equals the requested name's extension (ResourcesServiceImpl lines 444-480, 556-564), and verifyResourceName/checkResourceExists only test DB existence and storage existence (lines 232-235, 725-755) — they do not sanitize the path. The worker repeats the flaw: the DB-stored fullName is joined onto the task execution directory in TaskExecuteThread.downloadResource (lines 292-318, `new File(execLocalPath, fullName)` / `copyHdfsToLocal(..., execLocalPath + File.separator + fullName)`), with the map built from Resource.fullName in BaseTaskProcessor.getResourceFullNames (lines 417-445).
candidates.title: Resource-center path traversal: unvalidated currentDir/name/alias allow arbitrary file write/delete in resource storage and on API/worker hosts
candidates.trace: 1) `createResource`: fullName = `/` + name (line 189); `verifyFile` only compares extensions (444-480); `upload()` builds `<resource.upload.path>/<tenant>/resources/<fullName>` via HadoopUtils.getHdfsFileName (571) and calls copyLocalToHdfs(localFilename, hdfsFilename, true, true) (579) — `..` in `name` escapes the tenant directory in the configured storage. 2) `onlineCreateResource`: fullName from fileName+suffix+currentDir (892-893) is passed to uploadContentToHdfs (917) with the same unvalidated path. 3) `downloadResource`: hdfsFileName is read from the attacker-controlled fullName (1094) and the local destination is `<data.basedir>/download/<ts>/<alias>` with the raw alias (FileUtils.getDownloadFilename, 1096), then HadoopUtils.copyHdfsToLocal(hdfsFileName, localFileName, false, true) (1099) writes the attacker's HDFS content to an OS-resolved local path such as `/tmp/evil.sh` on the API server; the endpoint also performs no permission check on the resource (controller 450-452, service 1062). 4) `deleteResource`: HadoopUtils.delete(hdfsFilename, true) (712) recursively deletes the resolved traversal path. 5) Worker: master puts fullName into the task execution context (BaseTaskProcessor 439, TaskExecutionContextBuilder 61) and TaskExecuteThread.downloadResource (302, 309) writes execLocalPath + "/" + fullName, escaping the per-task execution directory.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed (no code executed, no tests run). Deployment-dependent: actual `resource.storage.type`, whether the API/worker/HDFS users can write the chosen target paths, and whether the storage and local filesystems are the same (`file:///` vs a separate HDFS). The `..` resolution behavior of the specific Hadoop/S3 FileSystem implementation was reasoned from Hadoop Path semantics, not executed. I could not map this code to a specific CVE/fix commit from the snapshot (no CVE metadata in the repository), so this is a code-evidence lead, not a verified CVE match.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-22 Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal')

coverage_summary: Reviewed the assigned snapshot using the source tools plus the P1 relation index. Source scope: 1430 visible files; the index parsed 854 Java files / 11452 symbols but is partial (23 source files missing from the index) and has no control-flow, data-flow or semantic resolution, so index hits were only used as navigation and every claim was re-checked in source text. Areas inspected in depth: dolphinscheduler-api controllers/services (Resources, ProcessDefinition, TaskDefinition, Executor, Logger, DataSource, Users, security/LDAP, interceptors, AppConfiguration), dolphinscheduler-service (ProcessService, permission checks), dolphinscheduler-server (master task processors incl. switch, worker TaskExecuteThread, log RPC processor, monitor, ProcessUtils), dolphinscheduler-common (FileUtils, HadoopUtils, RegexUtils, PropertyUtils, common.properties), dolphinscheduler-dao mappers/XML, dolphinscheduler-datasource-plugin processors/providers, dolphinscheduler-task-plugin (shell/python/datax/sql), alert plugins, and dolphinscheduler-python. I searched for command execution, Java serialization, Jackson polymorphic deserialization, YAML/XML parsing, MyBatis `${}` usage, path construction, and authentication/authorization gaps. Not exhaustively reviewed: the UI tree, all MyBatis statements, every task/datasource plugin, and the C (non-Java) parts; no builds, tests, or scanners were run and no runtime behavior was verified.
limitations: No code was executed, built, or tested; all findings are static source evidence, and the candidate is a lead rather than a confirmed vulnerability.
The P1 index is partial (23 source files absent, no data-flow/reachability analysis); cross-file call and route edges are syntactic candidates only.

Exploitability of the selected candidate depends on deployment configuration (`resource.storage.type` is NONE by default; API/worker/HDFS user permissions; whether storage FS is local or HDFS) that cannot be verified from the snapshot.
The exact CVE/fix mapping for this snapshot could not be established because no CVE, advisory, or patch metadata exists in the repository, and external lookups were out of scope.
I could not inspect runtime configuration of any real deployment, so impact severity (e.g. ability to overwrite executable scripts) remains bounded by filesystem permissions.

rejected_leads.lead: Switch task evaluates user-authored JavaScript condition with Nashorn (`SwitchTaskProcessor` line 164-168 -> `SwitchTaskUtils.evaluate` -> `engine.eval`, dolphinscheduler-server/.../SwitchTaskUtils.java lines 24-36), which permits Java interop and therefore arbitrary Java execution on the master host by a user who can edit a task definition.
rejected_leads.reason: Strong alternative lead (attacker-controlled input reaches a code-execution sink with no sandbox), but evaluating a JavaScript condition is the documented function of the switch task; Java interop is an inherent Nashorn capability rather than a broken check, so it is more plausibly classified as an intended-but-dangerous feature/hardening gap than as the repository's labeled vulnerability. Reported here for awareness, not selected.

rejected_leads.lead: Unauthenticated RPC log service: `LoggerRequestProcessor.process` (dolphinscheduler-server/.../LoggerRequestProcessor.java lines 67-124, 137-150) accepts GET_LOG_BYTES/VIEW_WHOLE_LOG/ROLL_VIEW_LOG/REMOVE_TAK_LOG commands whose `path` field is used directly with `new FileInputStream(filePath)` and `taskLogFile.delete()`, with no authentication or path restriction on the RPC port.
rejected_leads.reason: Real boundary concern (arbitrary file read/delete if port 50051 is reachable), but the RPC tier has no authentication anywhere by design and exploitation requires network access to an internal cluster port; impact is also bounded by the process user's file permissions. Not selected.

rejected_leads.lead: LDAP login (dolphinscheduler-api/.../security/impl/ldap/LdapService.java lines 82-118): the username is formatted into the LDAP search filter without escaping (filter injection), and there is no empty-password check before the bind (unauthenticated-bind semantics can accept a DN with an empty password).
rejected_leads.reason: Exploitability depends on LDAP server behavior/configuration (unauthenticated bind and filter semantics), so the impact is conditional rather than demonstrated by source alone; the password bind still gates ordinary injection. Not selected.

rejected_leads.lead: Python gateway exposes a Py4J GatewayServer without authentication, bound by default to 0.0.0.0:25333 (`PythonGatewayServer.run` lines 513-535, `PythonGatewayConfig` default `gateway.server.address:0.0.0.0`), which exposes gateway methods and the Py4J JVM view to any client that can reach the port.
rejected_leads.reason: Severe if exposed, but the remote Py4J gateway is the intended interface for pydolphinscheduler and the default bind is a configuration choice; treating it as the repository's vulnerability would require assuming an unintended trust boundary. Not selected.

rejected_leads.lead: MySQL datasource hardening gap: `MysqlDatasourceProcessor.createConnectionParams` filters dangerous keys only for the URL `other` string but copies the raw map into `props` (lines 88-89), which HikariCP passes to the driver as connection properties (`JdbcDataSourceProvider` lines 59-61), potentially re-enabling `autoDeserialize`/`allowLoadLocalInfile` for clients created through Hikari (e.g. SQL tasks).
rejected_leads.reason: Requires a malicious/attacker-controlled database server and driver/gadget assumptions, and the URL-level denylist/APPEND_PARAMS hardening is already present; impact could not be verified from source alone. Not selected.

rejected_leads.lead: Logger API IDOR: `LoggerServiceImpl.queryLog(int taskInstId, ...)` / `getLogBytes(int taskInstId)` (lines 100-127) perform no project or ownership check, so any authenticated user can read/download any task instance log by enumerating ids, while only the `/{projectCode}/...` variants verify permissions.
rejected_leads.reason: Credible authorization flaw, but impact is limited to log disclosure (task output may contain secrets) and is lower than the selected path-traversal chain. Not selected.

summary: Repository is Apache DolphinScheduler 2.0.5 (Java, Maven multi-module; 1430 visible files, 854 Java files parsed by the relation index, 23 files missing from the index). I traced attacker-controlled HTTP input into filesystem/storage operations across the API, service and worker layers. The strongest source-evidenced candidate is a path-traversal root cause in the resource center: request parameters (`currentDir`, `name`/`fileName`, and the stored resource `alias`) are concatenated into HDFS/S3/local storage paths and local file paths without any validation or normalization, letting an authenticated user escape the tenant resource directory and write/delete files in the configured resource storage, and write attacker-controlled files outside the task execution directory on API and worker hosts (potential code execution via overwritten scripts/config). Other plausible issues (switch-task Nashorn eval, unauthenticated log RPC file read/delete, LDAP login, Py4J python gateway, unfiltered MySQL Hikari props) are listed as rejected/unconfirmed leads; none was selected because each is either an intended capability, requires an internal network position, or depends on unverifiable runtime/driver conditions.
